content.heading: 9.4 Duality
content.paragraph: Associated with each canonical (maximization) linear programming problem is a related minimization problem, called the dual problem. In this setting, the canonical problem is called the primal problem. This section describes the dual problem and how it is solved, along with an interesting economic interpretation of the dual variables. The section concludes by showing how any matrix game can be solved using the primal and dual versions of a suitable linear programming problem.

Given vectors $\mathbf{c}$ in $\textbf{ℝ}^{n}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ in $\textbf{ℝ}^{m}$, and given an $m \times n$ matrix $A$, the canonical (primal) problem is to find $\mathbf{x}$ in $\textbf{ℝ}^{n}$ so as to maximize $f(\textbf{x}) = \textbf{c}^{T}\textbf{x}$ subject to the constraints $A\textbf{x} \leq \textbf{b}$ and $\textbf{x} \geq \textbf{0}$. The dual (minimization) problem is to find $\mathbf{y}$ in $\textbf{ℝ}^{m}$ so as to minimize $g(\textbf{y}) = \textbf{b}^{T}\textbf{y}$ subject to $A^{T}\textbf{y} \geq \textbf{c}$ and $\textbf{y} \geq \textbf{0}$:

image.alt: A table lists three constraints each for primal problem P and dual problem P asterisk.

content.paragraph: Observe that in forming the dual problem, the $c_{i}$ coefficients of $x_{i}$ in the objective function of the primal problem become the constants on the right-hand side of the constraint inequalities in the dual. Likewise, the numbers in the right-hand side of the constraint inequalities in the primal problem become the coefficients $b_{j}$ of $y_{j}$ in the objective function in the dual. Also, note that the direction of the constraint inequalities is reversed from $A\textbf{x} \leq \textbf{b}$ to $A^{T}\textbf{y} \geq \textbf{c}$. In both cases, the variables $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ are nonnegative.

content.paragraph: The variables in the dual problem have useful economic interpretations. For example, consider the problem of mixing nuts studied in Example 5 of Section 9.2 and Example 6 of Section 9.3:
Recall that $x_{1}$ is the number of boxes of the first mixture and $x_{2}$ is the number of boxes of the second mixture. Example 2 displayed the following dual problem:
If $\mathbf{\overline{x}}$ and $\mathbf{\overline{y}}$ are optimal solutions of these problems, then by the Duality Theorem, the maximum profit $f(\mathbf{\overline{x}})$ satisfies the equation

Suppose, for example, that the amount of cashews available was increased from $30$ pounds to $30 + h$ pounds. Then the profit would increase by $h{\overset{ˉ}{y}}_{1}$. Likewise, if the amount of cashews was decreased by $h$ pounds, then the profit would decrease by $h{\overset{ˉ}{y}}_{1}$. So ${\overset{ˉ}{y}}_{1}$ represents the value (per pound) of increasing or decreasing the amount of cashews available. This is usually referred to as the marginal value of the cashews. Similarly, ${\overset{ˉ}{y}}_{2}$ and ${\overset{ˉ}{y}}_{3}$ are the marginal values of the filberts and peanuts, respectively. These values indicate how much the company might be willing to pay for additional supplies of the various nuts.2

content.heading: Linear Programming and Matrix Games
content.paragraph: Let $A$ be an $m \times n$ payoff matrix for a matrix game, as in Section 9.1, and assume at first that each entry in $A$ is positive. Let $\mathbf{u}$ in $\textbf{ℝ}^{m}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ in $\textbf{ℝ}^{n}$ be the vectors whose coordinates are all equal to one, and consider the following linear programming problem $P$ and its dual $P^{\ast}$. (Notice that the roles of $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ are reversed, with $\mathbf{x}$ in $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{m}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ in $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$.)

The primal problem $P$ is feasible since $\textbf{y} = \textbf{0}$ satisfies the constraints. The dual problem $P^{\ast}$ is feasible since all the entries in $A^{T}$ are positive and $\mathbf{v}$ is a vector of $1\text{’s}$. By the Duality Theorem, there exist optimal solutions $\mathbf{\overline{y}}$ and $\mathbf{\overline{x}}$ such that $\textbf{v}^{T}\mathbf{\overline{y}} = \textbf{u}^{T}\mathbf{\overline{x}}$. Set

Since the entries in $A$ and $\mathbf{u}$ are positive, the inequality $A\textbf{y} \leq \textbf{u}$ has a nonzero solution $\mathbf{y}$ with $\textbf{y} \geq \textbf{0}\text{.}$ As a result, the $\text{λ}$ for the primal problem is positive. Let

It can be shown (Exercise 29) that $\mathbf{\hat{y}}$ is the optimal mixed strategy for the column player $C$ and $\mathbf{\hat{x}}$ is the optimal mixed strategy for the row player $R$. Furthermore, the value of the game is equal to $1\text{/}\text{λ}$.

Finally, if the payoff matrix $A$ has some entries that are not positive, add a fixed number, say $k$, to each entry to make the entries all positive. This will not change the optimal mixed strategies for the two players, and it will add an amount $k$ to the value of the game. [See Exercise 33(b) in Section 9.1.]

content.paragraph: Although matrix games are usually solved via linear programming, it is interesting that a linear programming problem can be reduced to a matrix game. If the programming problem has an optimal solution, then this solution is reflected in the solution of the matrix game. Suppose the problem is to maximize $\textbf{c}^{T}\textbf{x}$ subject to $A\textbf{x} \leq \textbf{b}$ and $\textbf{x} \geq \textbf{0}$, where $A$ is $m \times n$ with $m \leq n$. Let

and suppose that $M$ represents a matrix game and $\mathbf{s}$ is an optimal column strategy for $M$. The $(n + m + 1) \times (n + m + 1)$ matrix $M$ is skew-symmetric; that is, $M^{T} = - M$. It can be shown that in this case the optimal row strategy equals the optimal column strategy, the value of the game is $0$, and the maximum of the entries in the vector $M\textbf{s}$ is $0$. Observe that

paragraph.math: $$M\mathbf{s} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & A & {- \mathbf{b}} \\ {- A^{T}} & 0 & \mathbf{c} \\ \mathbf{b}^{T} & {- \mathbf{c}^{T}} & 0 \end{bmatrix}{\left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} \mathbf{\overline{y}} \\ \mathbf{\overline{x}} \\ z \end{array} \right\rbrack~} = ~{\begin{bmatrix} {A\overline{\mathbf{x}} - z\mathbf{b}} \\ {- A^{T}\overline{\mathbf{y}} + z\mathbf{c}} \\ {\mathbf{b}^{T}\overline{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{c}^{T}\overline{\mathbf{x}}} \end{bmatrix}~} \leq {~\left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} \mathbf{0} \\ \mathbf{0} \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack}$$

content.paragraph: Thus $A\mathbf{\overline{x}} \leq z\textbf{b}$, $A^{T}\textbf{y} \geq z\textbf{c},$ and $\textbf{b}^{T}\mathbf{\overline{y}} \leq \textbf{c}^{T}\mathbf{\overline{x}}$. Since the column strategy $\mathbf{s}$ is a probability vector, $z \geq 0$. It can be shown that if $z > 0$, then $\mathbf{\overline{x}}\text{/}z$ is an optimal solution for the primal (maximization) problem for $A\textbf{x} \leq \textbf{b}$, and $\mathbf{\overline{y}}\text{/}z$ is an optimal solution for the dual problem for $A^{T}\textbf{y} \geq \textbf{c}$. Also, if $z = 0,$ then the primal and dual problems have no optimal solutions.

In conclusion, the simplex method is a powerful tool in solving linear programming problems. Because a fixed procedure is followed, it lends itself well to using a computer for the tedious calculations involved. The algorithm presented here is not optimal for a computer, but many computer programs implement variants of the simplex method, and some programs even seek integer solutions. New methods developed in recent years take shortcuts through the interior of the feasible region instead of going from extreme point to extreme point. They are somewhat faster in certain situations (typically involving thousands of variables and constraints), but the simplex method is still the approach most widely used.

Mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer.

statement.paragraph: (T/F) The dual problem is to minimize $\textbf{y}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{m}$ subject to $A\textbf{y} \geq \textbf{c}$ and $\textbf{y} \geq \textbf{0}$.
(T/F) The dual of the dual problem is the original primal problem.
(T/F) If both the primal and the dual problems are feasible, then they both have optimal solutions.
(T/F) If either the primal or the dual problem has an optimal solution, then they both do.

(T/F) If $\overset{‾}{\textbf{x}}$ is an optimal solution to the primal problem and $\widehat{\textbf{y}}$ is a feasible solution to the dual problem such that $g(\widehat{\textbf{y}}) = f(\overset{‾}{\textbf{x}})$, then $g(\widehat{\textbf{y}})$ is an optimal solution to the dual problem.
(T/F) If the primal problem has an optimal solution, then the final tableau in the simplex method also gives the optimal solution to the dual problem.
(T/F) If a slack variable is in an optimal solution, then the marginal value of the item corresponding to its equation is positive.
(T/F) When a linear programming problem and its dual are used to solve a matrix game, the vectors $\textbf{u}$ and $\textbf{v}$ are unit.
